description:

starter: # Write the whole program here
solution:
count = int(input("How many marks? "))

        passes = passes + 1

with open("weather.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Sunny")

with open("weather.txt", "r") as f:
    print(f.read())
worked_example.key_idea: with open(name, mode) as f: opens the file for the indented lines under it, and closes it again afterwards.

title: Open and close
description: This program uses open() and close() instead of with. What will it print?
solution:
file = open("pets.txt", "w")
file.write("cat\n")
file.write("dog\n")
file.close()

file = open("pets.txt", "r")
print(file.read())
file.close()
hints: Each write() adds its text, and \n starts a new line.
close() finishes with the file; then it can be opened again and read() gives back what is in it.

worked_example.problem: A car park saves its spaces with open() and close() written out.

title: One line

worked_example.problem: A train timetable is read one line at a time.
worked_example.code:
with open("trains.txt", "w") as f:

worked_example.output:
Stop: York

Stop: Newcastle

title: Shopping app
description:
Arrange the lines so the program saves items until the user types done, then reads the file back, numbering each item, and prints how many there are.
Two lines are not needed.
solution:

    item = input("Item (or done): ")

        file.write(item + "\n")
        item = input("Item (or done): ")

        count = count + 1
        print(count, line.strip())

    if items[mid] == target:
        found = True
    elif items[mid] < target:
        low = mid + 1
    else:
        high = mid - 1
print(found)

starter: # Write the Pupil class, then read the pupils into a list

class Pupil:
    def __init__(self, name, mark):

class Jar:

title: Trace a direct change
description: Trace the program. One line changes _qty directly instead of using sell.
solution:
class Stock:
    def __init__(self, qty):
        self._qty = qty
        self._sold = 0

    def sell(self, n):
        if n <= self._qty:
            self._qty = self._qty - n
            self._sold = self._sold + n

shop = Stock(10)
shop.sell(4)
shop._qty = shop._qty - 3
shop.sell(5)
total = shop._qty + shop._sold
print(total)
hints: sell changes both _qty and _sold.
The direct change only changes _qty.
explainer: Taking 3 off _qty directly skips sell, so _sold is never updated and the stock left plus the stock sold no longer adds up to the start.

title: Trace the meter
description: Trace the program. use adds units and works out the cost; one line resets _units directly.
solution:
class Meter:
    def __init__(self):
        self._units = 0
        self._cost = 0

    def use(self, n):
        if n > 0:
            self._units = self._units + n
            self._cost = self._units * 3

m = Meter()
m.use(5)
m.use(-2)
m.use(4)
m._units = 0
m.use(1)
bill = m._cost
print(bill)
hints: use refuses a negative number.
After the direct reset, use works the cost out from the units again.
explainer: Setting _units to 0 directly resets the units without the class knowing, so the next use works the cost out from 1 unit only.

title: Fix the average mark
description: int() turns the text typed into a whole number: this is called casting. This program should read marks until -1 is typed, then print their average using //, for example Average: 15. It stops with an error. Fix it.
starter:
total = 0
count = 0
mark = int(input("Mark (-1 to stop): "))
while mark != -1:
    total = total + mark
    mark = int(input("Mark (-1 to stop): "))
print("Average:", total // count)
solution:
total = 0
count = 0
mark = int(input("Mark (-1 to stop): "))
while mark != -1:
    total = total + mark
    count = count + 1
    mark = int(input("Mark (-1 to stop): "))
print("Average:", total // count)
hints: The error is a ZeroDivisionError on the last line.
count never goes up inside the loop.
explainer: count is never increased inside the loop, so the division on the last line uses 0, and adding count = count + 1 to the loop fixes it.

title: Trace the orders
